script.opening: "Hi, I got out of prison yesterday and I've registered with you. The thing is they stopped all my medication at the gate — I've got nothing. I was on tablets for my head, for my fits, and I was on a methadone script in there. I don't know what I'm doing, I've got nowhere proper to stay, no money, and I'm starting to feel rough. Can you help me? I don't want to end up back where I was."

facts.text: HMP Leeds for 14 months. Released yesterday morning with a discharge grant and "a bit of paper" — you have lost it. You were told an appointment with the drug service "would be sorted" but nobody has rung.

"Olanzapine — 10, I think, at night — for my head. Something for my fits, levetiracetam, twice a day. And methadone, 50 ml every morning." Last doses were the morning before release, about 30 hours ago.

Sweaty, yawning, stomach cramps, runny nose, aching — "starting to rattle". Sleeping badly. No fits since about two years ago; last one was when you stopped the tablets before. You are not hearing voices at the moment "but I can feel myself getting wound up".
Used heroin for years before prison. Clean inside. "I've had a mate offer me some already. I said no. For now." You know your tolerance is low.

facts.topic: Mental health — only if asked directly
facts.text: Diagnosed with schizophrenia at 25; two admissions, last one six years ago. If asked about suicide: "Some days I think what's the point." No plan; you have not harmed yourself since prison; you would ring your sister if it got bad.
Sleeping on a friend's sofa for now, "but he uses, so it's not great". No money until benefits come through. Probation officer, Sarah, is expecting you on Thursday.
Epilepsy since childhood. Hepatitis C — "they treated it inside". No allergies. Smoke 20 a day.

Anxious, a bit jumpy, trying hard. If the doctor sounds like they will just "wait for your records", you panic: "I can't wait, I'll be using by the weekend." If they take you seriously, get the prison healthcare details, explain what can be sorted today (fits tablets, mental-health medicine, urgent drug service, naloxone) and help with housing, you calm down and cooperate — giving consent to contact the prison, probation and the drug service.

ice.ideas: "They've stopped my meds and I need them back today."
ice.concerns: "I don't want to end up back where I was" — using, unwell, or back inside. Underneath: having a fit or "losing it".
ice.expectations: "Can you help me?" You want your tablets and somebody to sort things with you.

cues: "I don't want to end up back where I was." — say in the opening.
"A mate's already offered me some." — say if asked about drugs.
"Some days I think what's the point." — say only if asked about your mood directly.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the post-release period as EXTREME risk (drug-related overdose death from lost tolerance, suicide, relapse, mental-health and seizure risk) and treats continuity of essential medication and support as an URGENT, potentially life-saving priority

Prioritises and acts on each medication with appropriate urgency: verifies prison medications (prison healthcare/records) and safely continues the ANTIPSYCHOTIC (relapse risk) and ANTIEPILEPTIC (seizure risk — not to be stopped abruptly), and routes OST/methadone via the drug service (verify, don’t prescribe blind)

Addresses the SOCIAL emergency: housing/homelessness, finance/benefits, and linkage to substance-misuse and mental-health services — using prison-release liaison/RECONNECT-type and homeless-health pathways where available
Carries out a MENTAL-HEALTH and RISK assessment (psychotic relapse, suicide/self-harm, substance relapse) and provides HARM REDUCTION (overdose risk/lost tolerance, naloxone)
Acts with genuine URGENCY/continuity rather than deferring — obtaining records and bridging essential medication safely the same day where possible, and not leaving him with "nothing"
Treats him with RESPECT and dignity — not as a difficult registration — hears the fear of relapse and being judged, and reassures him his health matters and he will be helped
Holds the safety boundaries (verify OST, don’t prescribe blind) while conveying genuine urgency and care, so he engages rather than disengages

Safety-nets and follows up: urgent verified medication continuity, wrap-around support arranged (housing/finance/substance/MH services), risk plan and crisis routes, harm-reduction/naloxone, and a close follow-up — continuity-as-care through a high-risk window

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you rang — you’ve done exactly the right thing, and I’m going to treat this as urgent, because the first days after getting out are when people most need looking after, not least. You matter, and I’m not going to leave you with nothing. Let’s sort this together."

"Let’s take the medications one at a time, because some can’t safely just stop. Your epilepsy tablet — stopping that suddenly can cause fits, so that’s a priority to continue. Your tablet for your head — stopping risks you becoming unwell again, so that too. And the methadone I have to continue the safe way through the drug team rather than write blind — but I’ll get that moving today. I’ll pull your prison records to confirm everything."

"Just as important — you said you’ve nowhere proper to stay and no money. That’s not separate from your health, it’s central to it, and there’s help I can connect you with today: housing support, sorting some money, and the teams who help people just out of prison. You shouldn’t be facing this with nothing."

"Can I check how you are in yourself — your mood, any thoughts of harming yourself, how the cravings are? … Thank you. One really important safety thing: your tolerance will have dropped inside, so using like before could be an overdose. Please don’t — and we’ll get you naloxone to be safe. If you’re ever at risk, that’s 999."

"I want you to hear this clearly: you’re not being passed around or judged. The opposite — I’m going to chase your records, get your essential medication continued safely today, link you with the drug team, and get you support for housing and money. We’re doing this now."

"So: I’ll get your prison medication records, continue what can’t safely wait, fast-track the methadone through the drug service, and connect you with release and housing support — and I’ll ring you back today with the plan. I want to see you again very soon to keep you safe through these next weeks. You rang frightened of ending up back where you were; my job is to make sure you don’t."

f.learning: The first weeks after prison release are an extreme-risk window — markedly elevated drug-related overdose death (lost tolerance after enforced abstinence/reduction), suicide, relapse, mental-health crisis and seizure risk — so being left with "nothing" is a dangerous gap to close urgently, and continuity of medication plus rapid wrap-around support is potentially life-saving. Triage each medication: continue the ANTIEPILEPTIC (abrupt stopping risks seizures) and ANTIPSYCHOTIC (stopping risks relapse) safely and urgently after verifying prison records, and route OST/methadone via the drug service (verify, don’t prescribe blind — same rule as bridging, plus overdose risk from lost tolerance). Address the intertwined SOCIAL emergency (homelessness, finance, substance/mental-health service linkage) via prison-release/RECONNECT-type and homeless-health pathways, carry out a mental-health/risk assessment, and provide harm reduction (overdose/naloxone). The examinable hidden agenda is fear of relapse and "ending up back where I was", shame and low self-worth, and an expectation of being judged/turned away; meet him with respect and genuine urgency — his life matters — hold the OST boundary while conveying care, and deliver continuity-as-life-saving-care with close follow-up. He is effectively homeless, penniless and unsupported — a social emergency intertwined with the medical one. Housing, benefits/finance, and substance/mental-health service linkage are core. Many areas have specific prison-release/RECONNECT-type liaison and homeless-health pathways. Addressing the destitution is part of preventing the bad outcomes.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG57 — Physical health of people in prison · NICE QS156 · NICE NG66 · NICE NG217 · NICE CG178 · DHSC Drug misuse and dependence: UK guidelines on clinical management (2017)
knowledge.summary: The weeks after release carry a sharply raised risk of death, mostly drug overdose from lost tolerance. Close the medication gap today: verify with prison healthcare, restart the antiepileptic and antipsychotic, route methadone through the drug service, give naloxone and overdose advice, and start housing and money support.

points.t: Mortality is markedly raised in the first weeks after release, driven by drug-related overdose after tolerance falls in custody, with raised suicide, relapse and mental-health crisis. Treat a medication gap in a recently released person as same-day work.

points.h: What should have happened at the gate
points.t: NICE NG57 and QS156 (statement 5): people leaving prison should go with at least 7 days of prescribed medicines or an FP10 prescription, and complex needs should be planned before release. Leaving with nothing is a care gap to fix, not his fault.

Phone the releasing prison’s healthcare team today for the medication record, last-dose times and the release summary. Once confirmed, prescribe the antiepileptic (NICE NG217: abrupt withdrawal risks seizures and status) and the antipsychotic (NICE CG178: stopping risks relapse). Doses per BNF and the prison record.

Confirm the methadone dose and the time of the last supervised dose with the prison, then hand over the same day to the community drug service (or a GP working under shared care). Missed doses lower tolerance quickly, so restarting at the old dose without checking can be fatal. NICE TA114 supports methadone or buprenorphine as maintenance options.

Explain lost tolerance in plain words: using what he used before could kill him. Make sure he has take-home naloxone (drug services and many pharmacies can supply it without a prescription) and knows not to use alone or mix with alcohol, benzodiazepines or gabapentinoids.

Ask directly about mood, suicidal thoughts, self-harm, voices or paranoia and cravings. NICE NG66 covers mental health for adults in contact with the criminal justice system: continuity of care and liaison with probation and community mental health teams.

Homelessness and no money raise every clinical risk. Refer to the local authority housing options team (Homelessness Reduction Act 2017), signpost Universal Credit with an advance, and use care-after-custody services such as NHS England RECONNECT where available.

dg.d: Checked identity and privacy by phone; open question; let him list what he was taking without rushing to a registration script.
Where he will sleep tonight, money, phone contact, drug use since release, support from anyone.
Same-day call to prison healthcare for the medication record and last doses; face-to-face review within days.
Opioid withdrawal vs other illness; risk of seizure from antiepileptic withdrawal; early psychotic relapse; low mood.
Asked directly about suicidal thoughts, self-harm, voices or paranoia, seizures since release, and use since release.
Named the problem clearly: an unsafe medication gap in the highest-risk weeks after release, with a social emergency on top.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Verify, then continue antiepileptic and antipsychotic today; methadone via the drug service, never blind; naloxone and overdose advice.
Housing options referral, Universal Credit with advance, care-after-custody liaison, mental-health support.
Call-back the same afternoon, face-to-face review within days, 999 for fit or overdose, crisis line for mental-health deterioration.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “feeling rough” (withdrawal) and “don’t want to end up back where I was” (relapse fear), and explored both.
Idea that he just needs his meds back; fear of relapse and of being turned away; expectation of help today.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "I don't want to end up back where I was" — using, unwell, or back inside. Underneath: having a fit or "losing it" — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello Lee, it’s Dr Patel from the surgery. Before anything else — can you confirm your date of birth for me, and are you somewhere you can talk?
model.why: Telephone identity check and privacy before a sensitive call

model.text: Yeah, I can talk. I got out yesterday and they’ve stopped all my meds. I’ve got nothing, and I’m starting to feel rough.

I’m really glad you rang, and you’ve done exactly the right thing. The first days after getting out are when people most need looking after, so I’m treating this as urgent today. Can you tell me what you were taking inside?
model.why: Meets him with respect and urgency, not as a difficult registration

model.text: Tablets for my head, tablets for my fits, and a methadone script. I don’t know the names. Nobody gave me anything when I walked out.
That’s fine — I’ll get the exact names and doses from the prison healthcare team. When did you last have each of them?
model.why: Establishes last doses to judge seizure, relapse and tolerance risk

model.text: Yesterday morning, before I left. I’ve had nothing since.
Thank you. The fits tablets first — have you had any fits, jerks or strange turns since yesterday?
model.why: Screens for early seizure risk from abrupt antiepileptic withdrawal

model.text: No. Just shaky and sweaty, and I can’t settle.
That sounds like it could be coming off the methadone. Has anyone offered you anything on the street, or have you used since you got out?
model.why: Recognises withdrawal and asks about use without judgement

model.text: Not yet. But I’m not going to lie, it’s in my head. I don’t want to end up back where I was.
I really respect you telling me that. Can I ask how you are in yourself — your mood, and whether you’ve had any thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life?
model.why: Direct suicide and self-harm risk question

model.text: I’m scared, and I don’t know what I’m doing. I’m not going to do anything stupid.
And the illness your head tablets are for — any voices, or feeling people are against you, since you stopped?
Not right now, no.
You said you don’t want to end up back where you were. What worries you most about the next few days?
model.why: Follows the key cue into his fear of relapse

model.text: That I’ll get turned away everywhere, end up using, and it all goes wrong again. People look at you different when you’ve been inside.

I hear that, and I want you to know you’re not being judged here. You rang for help, and you’re going to get it. You also said you’ve nowhere proper to stay and no money — where are you sleeping tonight?
model.why: Counters the expectation of rejection and moves to the social emergency

model.text: I don’t know yet. Nowhere proper.

Here’s how I see it. Three medicines, and none of them should just stop. The fits tablet can’t stop suddenly, because that can bring on seizures. The tablet for your head protects you from getting unwell again. So as soon as the prison confirms the doses — I’m ringing them straight after this call — I’ll get both prescribed today.
model.why: Triages the antiepileptic and antipsychotic for same-day continuation after verification

model.text: And the methadone?

I have to do the methadone the safe way, which means confirming your exact dose and handing you over to the local drug service today, so they can restart it properly. I’m not fobbing you off — getting it wrong is how people die, and I want you around.
model.why: Holds the OST boundary while showing care, so he stays engaged

model.text: Fair enough. As long as it’s today.

One really important safety thing. Your tolerance will have dropped inside, so using the amount you used before could stop your breathing. Please don’t use — and if you do, never alone, and never with drink or other tablets. I’m going to make sure you have a naloxone kit today. Do you know what that is?
model.why: Harm reduction: lost tolerance, not using alone, naloxone

model.text: I think so — the stuff that brings you round?

Exactly. So here’s my plan, and tell me if it works for you. One: I ring the prison now and prescribe your fits and head tablets to a pharmacy near you. Two: I refer you to the drug service today for the methadone and a naloxone kit. Three: I refer you to the council’s housing team and give you the number for Universal Credit, including an advance payment. Four: I ask the care-after-custody team to contact you. Which pharmacy is easiest?
model.why: Concrete same-day wrap-around plan: medicines, OST, housing, money, liaison

model.text: There’s one near where I am.
Good. Is this the best number to reach you on? I’ll ring you back this afternoon once I’ve spoken to the prison, so you’re not left wondering.
model.why: Secures a contact route for a patient with no fixed address

model.text: Yeah, keep it on me. Thanks.

If you have a fit, or someone you’re with won’t wake up or is breathing strangely, that’s 999. If your head gets bad, or you start thinking about harming yourself, ring NHS 111 and choose the mental health option, or come straight here. Can you tell me back what’s happening today?
model.why: Specific safety-net with crisis routes and teach-back

model.text: You call the prison, sort my tablets at the chemist, drug team for the methadone and the naloxone, housing and the money. And 999 if I fit.

Perfect. I’d also like to see you in person in the next few days, so we can go through everything properly. You rang frightened of ending up back where you were — my job is to help make sure you don’t.
model.why: Books close follow-up and closes on his own words

model.text: Nobody’s said that to me in a long time. Cheers, doc.

social.t: No fixed address and no money make missed doses, drug use and crisis far more likely. Housing, Universal Credit (an advance can be requested) and a working phone number are part of the treatment.
People leaving prison often expect to be judged or turned away. A respectful, practical first call is what keeps him engaged with services.

legal.t: Local authorities must help people who are homeless or threatened with homelessness, and certain public bodies, including prisons and probation, have a duty to refer. The GP can signpost or refer to the housing options team.
Methadone is a Schedule 2 controlled drug (Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001). Instalment and supervised dispensing is arranged by the prescribing service; verify the regimen before any prescription.
Since 2015, UK regulations allow drug services to supply naloxone without a prescription for use in an emergency. Make sure he leaves with a kit or knows where to get one today.

professional.t: GP registration does not need proof of address. GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: treat patients fairly, without discrimination, and make sure care continues when responsibility passes between services.
GMC prescribing guidance: prescribe only when you have enough information about the patient’s current medicines. That is the reason to verify with the prison today, not a reason to wait.

community.t: Community drug and alcohol service, care-after-custody liaison (NHS England RECONNECT where commissioned), probation, community mental health team, homeless health services and local charities.

redFlags: Seizures, jerks or funny turns since the antiepileptic stopped
Suicidal thoughts, self-harm, voices or paranoia returning
Use of opioids or other drugs since release — overdose risk from lost tolerance
psychosocial: Where he is sleeping tonight, money, and a working phone number
Who else is involved: probation, drug service, anyone supportive
Cravings, withdrawal and what he has been offered since release
ice: Idea: “I just need my meds back.”
Concern: relapse, “ending up back where I was”, and being turned away
Expectation: help today, not another queue

playbook.diagnosis: Name it plainly: “You’ve been left without three medicines that can’t safely stop, at the time people are most at risk after release. That’s urgent, and we’re fixing it today.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of the first weeks out as walking a narrow bridge. Your medicines, somewhere to stay and people on your side are the handrails. Right now you’ve got none, so we’re putting them back up today.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me you don’t want to end up back where you were. Everything in this plan is aimed at exactly that.”
management.psychosocial: Housing options referral, Universal Credit with an advance, care-after-custody liaison, and a call-back to the number he gives — he has nowhere fixed to receive letters.
sharedPlan: Ring prison healthcare today for the medication record and last doses
Prescribe the antiepileptic and antipsychotic once verified; methadone via the drug service, never blind
Naloxone kit and lost-tolerance advice; mental-health risk plan
safetyNet: 999 for a seizure, or if someone is unrousable or breathing abnormally
NHS 111 mental health option or the surgery for low mood, suicidal thoughts or relapse; call-back this afternoon and review within days

pitfalls.intro: This station is not about knowing drug names. It is failed by treating a life-threatening gap as routine admin, by prescribing unsafely under pressure, or by ignoring the homelessness that drives the risk.

items.fail: Booking a routine new-patient check and waiting for records to arrive by post.
items.why: “Did not recognise the urgency of the presentation.” Overdose deaths cluster in the first weeks after release; a seizure can follow abrupt antiepileptic withdrawal.
items.fix: Say it and do it: “I’m ringing the prison now and I’ll call you back this afternoon.” Same-day verification, same-day prescribing.

items.fail: Writing the methadone at the dose he remembers to be helpful.
items.why: Unverified OST with falling tolerance can kill. Examiners mark this as unsafe management however kind the intent.
items.fix: Verify the dose and last-dose time with the prison and hand over to the drug service today. Explain why, so the boundary reads as care.

items.fail: No question about suicide, voices or drug use since release.
items.why: “Did not assess risk.” He has a psychotic illness, has stopped treatment and is homeless — all risk multipliers.
items.fix: Ask directly and kindly: “Any thoughts of harming yourself? Anything telling you people are against you? Have you used since you got out?”

items.fail: Never mentioning naloxone or lost tolerance.
items.why: Harm reduction is a core management point in this station and one of the simplest life-saving actions available.
items.fix: “Your tolerance has dropped — the old amount could stop your breathing. Never use alone, and let’s get you a naloxone kit today.”

items.fail: A guarded, procedural tone — “we have policies about controlled drugs” — that confirms his fear of being judged.
items.why: “Did not respond to the patient’s concerns.” If he disengages today, he may use tonight.
items.fix: Lead with warmth: “You’ve done the right thing ringing, and you’re not being judged.” Then explain the safety steps as care for him.

items.fail: Ending the call with no working contact route for a man with no address.
items.why: “Follow-up not arranged.” A plan that depends on a letter or an unanswered number will not happen.
items.fix: Confirm the phone number, the pharmacy he can reach, a call-back time today, and a face-to-face review within days.

timeMap.d: Identity and privacy check. Tell him early that you’re treating this as urgent — it buys his trust for the rest of the call.
Last doses of each medicine; any seizures; withdrawal; use since release; mood, suicide, voices. Where he sleeps tonight.
Follow “I don’t want to end up back where I was” — fear of relapse and of being turned away.
Ring prison today; restart antiepileptic and antipsychotic once verified; drug service for methadone; naloxone; housing, money, care-after-custody.
999 for fits or overdose, crisis line, call-back this afternoon, face-to-face in days, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Treats it as a routine registration or books him in next week; prescribes methadone blind or refuses all medication until records arrive; never asks about suicide, use since release or where he sleeps; no naloxone or overdose warning; no call-back.
wordPics.pass: Recognises the urgency; verifies with the prison and restarts the antiepileptic and antipsychotic promptly; routes methadone via the drug service; asks about risk; gives overdose advice; signposts housing and benefits; arranges follow-up.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explains the lost-tolerance risk in plain words and secures naloxone; holds the methadone boundary so warmly that he stays engaged; sets a same-day call-back on a working number; links him to care-after-custody support; closes on his own fear and he leaves feeling someone is on his side.

avoid.dont: “You’ll need to book a new-patient check first, and we can’t do anything until your records come through.”
avoid.instead: “I’m ringing the prison straight after this call so we can get your tablets going today.”
avoid.why: A routine delay in the highest-risk window after release is a safety failure.

avoid.dont: “I’ll just write you the same methadone dose you were on.”
avoid.instead: “I’ll confirm your exact dose and get the drug service to restart it with you today — that’s how we keep you safe.”
avoid.why: Prescribing OST blind with falling tolerance risks a fatal overdose.

avoid.dont: “Housing isn’t really something the GP can help with.”
avoid.instead: “Where you sleep tonight is part of your health, so I’m referring you to the housing team now.”
avoid.why: The social emergency drives the clinical risk; ignoring it loses Tasks and Relating marks.

I really respect you telling me that. Can I ask how you are in yourself — your mood, and whether you’ve had any thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life?
SCA_MODELS.why: Direct suicide and self-harm risk question

SCA_MODELS.text: I’m scared, and I don’t know what I’m doing. I’m not going to do anything stupid.
And the illness your head tablets are for — any voices, or feeling people are against you, since you stopped?
Not right now, no.
You said you don’t want to end up back where you were. What worries you most about the next few days?
SCA_MODELS.why: Follows the key cue into his fear of relapse

SCA_MODELS.text: That I’ll get turned away everywhere, end up using, and it all goes wrong again. People look at you different when you’ve been inside.

I hear that, and I want you to know you’re not being judged here. You rang for help, and you’re going to get it. You also said you’ve nowhere proper to stay and no money — where are you sleeping tonight?
SCA_MODELS.why: Counters the expectation of rejection and moves to the social emergency

SCA_MODELS.text: I don’t know yet. Nowhere proper.

Here’s how I see it. Three medicines, and none of them should just stop. The fits tablet can’t stop suddenly, because that can bring on seizures. The tablet for your head protects you from getting unwell again. So as soon as the prison confirms the doses — I’m ringing them straight after this call — I’ll get both prescribed today.
SCA_MODELS.why: Triages the antiepileptic and antipsychotic for same-day continuation after verification

SCA_MODELS.text: And the methadone?

I have to do the methadone the safe way, which means confirming your exact dose and handing you over to the local drug service today, so they can restart it properly. I’m not fobbing you off — getting it wrong is how people die, and I want you around.
SCA_MODELS.why: Holds the OST boundary while showing care, so he stays engaged

SCA_MODELS.text: Fair enough. As long as it’s today.

One really important safety thing. Your tolerance will have dropped inside, so using the amount you used before could stop your breathing. Please don’t use — and if you do, never alone, and never with drink or other tablets. I’m going to make sure you have a naloxone kit today. Do you know what that is?
SCA_MODELS.why: Harm reduction: lost tolerance, not using alone, naloxone

SCA_MODELS.text: I think so — the stuff that brings you round?

Exactly. So here’s my plan, and tell me if it works for you. One: I ring the prison now and prescribe your fits and head tablets to a pharmacy near you. Two: I refer you to the drug service today for the methadone and a naloxone kit. Three: I refer you to the council’s housing team and give you the number for Universal Credit, including an advance payment. Four: I ask the care-after-custody team to contact you. Which pharmacy is easiest?
SCA_MODELS.why: Concrete same-day wrap-around plan: medicines, OST, housing, money, liaison

SCA_MODELS.text: There’s one near where I am.
Good. Is this the best number to reach you on? I’ll ring you back this afternoon once I’ve spoken to the prison, so you’re not left wondering.
SCA_MODELS.why: Secures a contact route for a patient with no fixed address

SCA_MODELS.text: Yeah, keep it on me. Thanks.

If you have a fit, or someone you’re with won’t wake up or is breathing strangely, that’s 999. If your head gets bad, or you start thinking about harming yourself, ring NHS 111 and choose the mental health option, or come straight here. Can you tell me back what’s happening today?
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety-net with crisis routes and teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: You call the prison, sort my tablets at the chemist, drug team for the methadone and the naloxone, housing and the money. And 999 if I fit.

Perfect. I’d also like to see you in person in the next few days, so we can go through everything properly. You rang frightened of ending up back where you were — my job is to help make sure you don’t.
SCA_MODELS.why: Books close follow-up and closes on his own words

SCA_MODELS.text: Nobody’s said that to me in a long time. Cheers, doc.

SCA_STEM.name: Lee Marwood
pmh: New registration — previous records not yet received
Patient reports: psychotic illness, epilepsy, opioid dependence on opioid substitution treatment in custody
meds: Reported in custody: an antipsychotic, an antiepileptic and methadone — names and doses unconfirmed
SCA_STEM.recent: Released from prison yesterday. Registered with the practice this morning. No fixed address recorded.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone call: “They stopped all my medication at the gate — I’ve got nothing.”

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG57 — Physical health of people in prison · NICE QS156 · NICE NG66 · NICE NG217 · NICE CG178 · DHSC Drug misuse and dependence: UK guidelines on clinical management (2017)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: The weeks after release carry a sharply raised risk of death, mostly drug overdose from lost tolerance. Close the medication gap today: verify with prison healthcare, restart the antiepileptic and antipsychotic, route methadone through the drug service, give naloxone and overdose advice, and start housing and money support.

points.t: Mortality is markedly raised in the first weeks after release, driven by drug-related overdose after tolerance falls in custody, with raised suicide, relapse and mental-health crisis. Treat a medication gap in a recently released person as same-day work.

points.h: What should have happened at the gate
points.t: NICE NG57 and QS156 (statement 5): people leaving prison should go with at least 7 days of prescribed medicines or an FP10 prescription, and complex needs should be planned before release. Leaving with nothing is a care gap to fix, not his fault.

Phone the releasing prison’s healthcare team today for the medication record, last-dose times and the release summary. Once confirmed, prescribe the antiepileptic (NICE NG217: abrupt withdrawal risks seizures and status) and the antipsychotic (NICE CG178: stopping risks relapse). Doses per BNF and the prison record.

Confirm the methadone dose and the time of the last supervised dose with the prison, then hand over the same day to the community drug service (or a GP working under shared care). Missed doses lower tolerance quickly, so restarting at the old dose without checking can be fatal. NICE TA114 supports methadone or buprenorphine as maintenance options.

Explain lost tolerance in plain words: using what he used before could kill him. Make sure he has take-home naloxone (drug services and many pharmacies can supply it without a prescription) and knows not to use alone or mix with alcohol, benzodiazepines or gabapentinoids.

Ask directly about mood, suicidal thoughts, self-harm, voices or paranoia and cravings. NICE NG66 covers mental health for adults in contact with the criminal justice system: continuity of care and liaison with probation and community mental health teams.

Homelessness and no money raise every clinical risk. Refer to the local authority housing options team (Homelessness Reduction Act 2017), signpost Universal Credit with an advance, and use care-after-custody services such as NHS England RECONNECT where available.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Checked identity and privacy by phone; open question; let him list what he was taking without rushing to a registration script.
Where he will sleep tonight, money, phone contact, drug use since release, support from anyone.
Picked up “feeling rough” (withdrawal) and “don’t want to end up back where I was” (relapse fear), and explored both.
Idea that he just needs his meds back; fear of relapse and of being turned away; expectation of help today.
Same-day call to prison healthcare for the medication record and last doses; face-to-face review within days.
Opioid withdrawal vs other illness; risk of seizure from antiepileptic withdrawal; early psychotic relapse; low mood.
Asked directly about suicidal thoughts, self-harm, voices or paranoia, seizures since release, and use since release.
Named the problem clearly: an unsafe medication gap in the highest-risk weeks after release, with a social emergency on top.
Verify, then continue antiepileptic and antipsychotic today; methadone via the drug service, never blind; naloxone and overdose advice.
Housing options referral, Universal Credit with advance, care-after-custody liaison, mental-health support.
Call-back the same afternoon, face-to-face review within days, 999 for fit or overdose, crisis line for mental-health deterioration.

social.t: No fixed address and no money make missed doses, drug use and crisis far more likely. Housing, Universal Credit (an advance can be requested) and a working phone number are part of the treatment.
People leaving prison often expect to be judged or turned away. A respectful, practical first call is what keeps him engaged with services.

legal.t: Local authorities must help people who are homeless or threatened with homelessness, and certain public bodies, including prisons and probation, have a duty to refer. The GP can signpost or refer to the housing options team.
Methadone is a Schedule 2 controlled drug (Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001). Instalment and supervised dispensing is arranged by the prescribing service; verify the regimen before any prescription.
Since 2015, UK regulations allow drug services to supply naloxone without a prescription for use in an emergency. Make sure he leaves with a kit or knows where to get one today.

professional.t: GP registration does not need proof of address. GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: treat patients fairly, without discrimination, and make sure care continues when responsibility passes between services.
GMC prescribing guidance: prescribe only when you have enough information about the patient’s current medicines. That is the reason to verify with the prison today, not a reason to wait.

community.t: Community drug and alcohol service, care-after-custody liaison (NHS England RECONNECT where commissioned), probation, community mental health team, homeless health services and local charities.

redFlags: Seizures, jerks or funny turns since the antiepileptic stopped
Suicidal thoughts, self-harm, voices or paranoia returning
Use of opioids or other drugs since release — overdose risk from lost tolerance
psychosocial: Where he is sleeping tonight, money, and a working phone number
Who else is involved: probation, drug service, anyone supportive
Cravings, withdrawal and what he has been offered since release
ice: Idea: “I just need my meds back.”
Concern: relapse, “ending up back where I was”, and being turned away
Expectation: help today, not another queue

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Name it plainly: “You’ve been left without three medicines that can’t safely stop, at the time people are most at risk after release. That’s urgent, and we’re fixing it today.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of the first weeks out as walking a narrow bridge. Your medicines, somewhere to stay and people on your side are the handrails. Right now you’ve got none, so we’re putting them back up today.”

management.reflectIce: “You told me you don’t want to end up back where you were. Everything in this plan is aimed at exactly that.”
management.psychosocial: Housing options referral, Universal Credit with an advance, care-after-custody liaison, and a call-back to the number he gives — he has nowhere fixed to receive letters.
sharedPlan: Ring prison healthcare today for the medication record and last doses
Prescribe the antiepileptic and antipsychotic once verified; methadone via the drug service, never blind
Naloxone kit and lost-tolerance advice; mental-health risk plan
safetyNet: 999 for a seizure, or if someone is unrousable or breathing abnormally
NHS 111 mental health option or the surgery for low mood, suicidal thoughts or relapse; call-back this afternoon and review within days

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is not about knowing drug names. It is failed by treating a life-threatening gap as routine admin, by prescribing unsafely under pressure, or by ignoring the homelessness that drives the risk.

items.fail: Booking a routine new-patient check and waiting for records to arrive by post.
items.why: “Did not recognise the urgency of the presentation.” Overdose deaths cluster in the first weeks after release; a seizure can follow abrupt antiepileptic withdrawal.
items.fix: Say it and do it: “I’m ringing the prison now and I’ll call you back this afternoon.” Same-day verification, same-day prescribing.

items.fail: Writing the methadone at the dose he remembers to be helpful.
items.why: Unverified OST with falling tolerance can kill. Examiners mark this as unsafe management however kind the intent.
items.fix: Verify the dose and last-dose time with the prison and hand over to the drug service today. Explain why, so the boundary reads as care.

items.fail: No question about suicide, voices or drug use since release.
items.why: “Did not assess risk.” He has a psychotic illness, has stopped treatment and is homeless — all risk multipliers.
items.fix: Ask directly and kindly: “Any thoughts of harming yourself? Anything telling you people are against you? Have you used since you got out?”

items.fail: Never mentioning naloxone or lost tolerance.
items.why: Harm reduction is a core management point in this station and one of the simplest life-saving actions available.
items.fix: “Your tolerance has dropped — the old amount could stop your breathing. Never use alone, and let’s get you a naloxone kit today.”

items.fail: A guarded, procedural tone — “we have policies about controlled drugs” — that confirms his fear of being judged.
items.why: “Did not respond to the patient’s concerns.” If he disengages today, he may use tonight.
items.fix: Lead with warmth: “You’ve done the right thing ringing, and you’re not being judged.” Then explain the safety steps as care for him.

items.fail: Ending the call with no working contact route for a man with no address.
items.why: “Follow-up not arranged.” A plan that depends on a letter or an unanswered number will not happen.
items.fix: Confirm the phone number, the pharmacy he can reach, a call-back time today, and a face-to-face review within days.
